title: Change in Students' Educational Expectations: A Meta-Analysis esearchgate.net/publication/358658746_Change_in_Students'_Educational_Expectations_-_A_Meta-A nalysis
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 16, 2024 — original paper: https://www.r
summary: Barton summarises a 2022 meta-analysis by Pinquart and Pietzsch that pooled 91 longitudinal studies tracking how students' educational expectations shift from childhood into young adulthood. The headline finding is that expectations about final degree attainment stay relatively stable over time, but expectations about near-term grades decline steadily and significantly. That decline in grade expectations is sharpest in the US and Canada, countries with the largest gap between what students expect and what they actually achieve, and is most pronounced around age 20, coinciding with the transition out of school. Barton draws out that students recalibrate more readily around frequent, direct feedback like grades than around distant outcomes like a final qualification, and highlights the study's caution that deliberately lowering overly optimistic expectations can backfire, sometimes even reducing achievement.
points: Students recalibrate grade expectations far more readily than degree-attainment expectations, likely because grades come with frequent, direct feedback.
The expectation-achievement gap, and the resulting decline in expectations, is largest in the US and Canada specifically.
The steepest drop in expectations occurs around age 20, during the transition from school to university, apprenticeship, or work.
An intervention aimed at lowering students' unrealistic expectations backfired, correlating with lower academic achievement rather than better calibration.
quotes: Researchers analyzed 91 longitudinal studies, finding that while expectations about highest educational degree remained relatively stable, expectations regarding future grades declined significantly.
This decline was more pronounced in the U.S. and Canada, countries with larger discrepancies between expected and actual educational attainment.
Further analysis revealed that age was a significant moderator, with the strongest decline in expectations occurring around age 20.
Students are more likely to adjust their expectations about their grades in the near future than about attaining a final degree later on.
Reductions in students' expectations are most obvious in late adolescence, when students transition from high school to university, apprenticeships, or jobs.

Positive educational expectations tend to be socially desirable (Jerrim, 2014) and may be a source of striving for success but may also be a source of academic stress and disappointment (Pinquart & Ebeling, 2020a).
